items.value: Dheera Shankarabharanam is the Carnatic raga corresponding to Hindustani Bilawal
items.reasoning: Bilawal is the Hindustani scale of all shuddha (natural) swaras, i.e. the natural major scale; its Carnatic counterpart is the 29th melakarta, Dheera Shankarabharanam, which uses exactly the same seven natural notes. The other three map elsewhere: Nat Bhairavi (20th melakarta) corresponds to Hindustani Asavari, Hanumatodi (8th) to Hindustani Bhairavi, and Kamavardhini or Pantuvarali (51st) to Puriya Dhanashri/Poorvi.

items.value: The overvalued 1s 6d rupee was fixed to ease the sterling cost of remittances out of India and to protect India's standing as a borrower in London
items.reasoning: The Hilton-Young Commission fixed the rupee at 1s 6d rather than the 1s 4d Indian opinion demanded. An artificially high rupee meant that fewer rupees were needed to buy the sterling required for the Home Charges, pensions and the repatriated profits of British firms, and it kept India's credit good in the London money market. Option C is the opposite of the effect, since an overvalued currency makes exports such as cotton dearer abroad; option B is a side-effect that the British would not have adopted the policy for. RUNNER-UP: D. The Commission did also recommend a gold bullion standard, so a reviewer who reads the item as asking about the monetary-standard rationale rather than the fiscal one would pick D; D would win if the question is about why the rate was pegged at all rather than why it was pegged high.

items.value: The Pali coin-names plus the punch-marked silver coins are evidence for both the rise of towns and the shift to a money economy
items.reasoning: The Pali references to kahapana, nikkha, kamsa and kakanika, corroborated by large finds of silver punch-marked coins, are the standard evidence for the monetisation of exchange in the sixth-to-fourth centuries BC. Coinage is also one of the defining markers of the second urbanisation of the middle Ganga plain, because regular coined money presupposes the specialised craft production, market exchange and trade on which the new towns rested. RUNNER-UP: B. If the examiner reads the coin evidence narrowly, as speaking only to how exchange was conducted and not to where people lived, then 2 alone follows and B wins; C requires accepting coinage as an indirect indicator of urbanism, which is the usual textbook treatment.

items.value: Huchimalligudi at Aihole and the Dashavatara temple at Deogarh have Nagara shikharas; Malegitti Shivalaya and Virupaksha are Dravida
items.reasoning: The Dashavatara temple at Deogarh is a Gupta-period shrine carrying one of the earliest surviving curvilinear Nagara towers. The Huchimalligudi at Aihole is the early Chalukyan experiment with the northern rekha-prasada shikhara, and is cited precisely for introducing that form in the Deccan. By contrast the Malegitti Shivalaya at Badami and the Virupaksha temple at Pattadakal, the latter modelled on the Kailasanatha at Kanchipuram, are both Dravida vimanas with stepped, storeyed superstructures.

items.value: Yaksha is not one of the four Jaina gatis; the four are deva, manushya, tiryancha and naraki
items.reasoning: Jaina cosmology divides all embodied existence into four gatis or states of birth: deva (heavenly beings), manushya (humans), tiryancha (animals and plants) and naraki (hell beings). Yakshas are attendant demi-gods who appear in Jaina iconography as shasanadevatas beside the Tirthankaras, but they fall within the deva category and are not a separate form of existence.

items.value: The Hallisalasya panel at Bagh depicts a group folk dance
items.reasoning: The best-known paintings of the Bagh caves are in Cave 4, the Rang Mahal, whose celebrated panel shows a band of dancers and musicians. Hallisa or hallisaka is a circular group dance performed by women, and lasya is its graceful mode; the panel is therefore identified as a joyous folk dance scene, not a devotional or narrative subject. Buddha in meditation, Shiva and Parvati on Kailasa, and the churning of the ocean are all subjects of other sites.

items.value: All three statements about the spread of place-value notation are correct
items.reasoning: The earliest dated Indian epigraphic use of decimal place-value numerals is the Gujarat copper-plate grant of AD 595-96, dated in year 346 of the Chedi era. Place-value numerals become general in Indian inscriptions from the ninth century, the Gwalior inscription of AD 876 with its zero being the classic instance. And Sanskrit inscriptions in South-east Asia carry place-value numerals from the seventh century, the Cambodian and Old Malay records of AD 683 being the earliest known. RUNNER-UP: C. Statement 1 is the only one that could fail, and only on the naming: if the examiner treats the AD 595 grant as the Sankheda plate and holds the Mankani plates to be a different record, statement 1 becomes false and C wins.

items.value: Inferences 1 and 2 follow; inference 3 does not, because private wells and bathing platforms indicate private rather than common property
items.reasoning: Spindle-whorls scattered through the houses with no spinning wheels show that thread was drawn by hand-spindle inside the home, which is slow and laborious work, so inference 1 follows from statement I. Graduated scales and a standardised system of weights are a genuine achievement in measurement, so inference 2 follows from statement II. Inference 3 is the reverse of what statement III says: houses with their own wells, their own bathing platforms and large private courtyards point to individual household property and to differences of wealth, not to a common property system.

items.value: Bardoli was against a land-revenue enhancement while the Eka movement was against excessive rents
items.reasoning: The Bardoli Satyagraha of 1928, led by Vallabhbhai Patel in Surat district, was a refusal to pay a steep enhancement of the land-revenue assessment. The Eka or unity movement of 1921-22 in the Awadh districts of Hardoi, Bahraich, Sitapur and Barabanki was a protest by tenants against rents pitched far above the recorded rates and against oppression by thikadars. A is wrong because the Congress withdrew from Eka, whose leadership passed to Madari Pasi, while Bardoli was a Congress-led campaign from the start; B is wrong because Eka was directed against the taluqdars and Bardoli was a movement of peasant proprietors, not landless labourers; D misplaces both, since Eka was in Awadh and Bardoli in south Gujarat, not Saurashtra.

items.value: Only the pulley-and-pail evidence and the pre-Rigvedic use of the ox support the claims about well irrigation and animal-drawn water-lifting
items.reasoning: The two assertions are specifically that wells extended cultivation away from the flood plains, and that draught animals were used to raise the water. Item 1, the ashma chakra or stone pulley wheel and the ahava or strapped pails, is the direct technological evidence for lifting water from a well, and supports both. Item 3, the use of the ox before the Rigveda for ploughing and drawing carts, establishes that the draught-animal power assumed in the second assertion was already available. Item 2 concerns axes and sickles, which belong to forest clearance and harvesting and say nothing about wells or about lifting water, so it supports neither assertion.

items.value: The shared dolphin species in the Indus and Ganga systems is the basis for inferring a Pleistocene connection between them
items.reasoning: The assertion is about the Pleistocene, a geological epoch many millennia before any Indian text, so the Nadi-sukta of the Rigveda cannot be evidence for it; the Rigvedic river list bears on the second millennium BC at the earliest. The biogeographical argument is what does the work: the occurrence of the same river dolphin in both the Indus and the Ganga drainages is hard to explain unless the two systems were once joined, which is exactly the kind of tributary transfer the assertion describes. Robert Bruce Foote was a geologist of Indian prehistory whose fieldwork lay mainly in the peninsula, not in a survey of the Sutlej and the Yamuna. RUNNER-UP: C. C would win if the examiner intends the assertion to rest on textual and survey evidence rather than on biogeography, treating the dolphin point as a modern aside; the Pleistocene dating in the stem is what argues against that.

items.value: The empty seat stands for the Buddha's meditation
items.reasoning: Early Buddhist art at Bharhut and Sanchi is aniconic and represents the Buddha through symbols rather than a human figure. Each symbol carries a fixed reference: the wheel stands for the first sermon at Sarnath, the stupa for the mahaparinibbana, the riderless horse for the great departure, the Bodhi tree for the enlightenment, and the empty seat or vacant throne for the Buddha's meditation.

items.value: Only Parushni-Ravi is correct; Vitasta is the Jhelum, Asikni the Chenab, and the Beas is the Vipasha, not the Yavyavati
items.reasoning: The standard Rigvedic identifications are Vitasta with the Jhelum and Asikni with the Chenab, so pairs 1 and 2 have simply been exchanged. Parushni is the Ravi, on whose banks the Battle of the Ten Kings was fought, so pair 3 is right. The Beas is the Vipasha or Vipas; Yavyavati is a much less certainly located stream and is not the Beas, so pair 4 fails. Only 3 stands.

items.value: Amaravati stood in the lower Krishna valley and its sculpture shaped later South Indian and overseas art, but it was not smaller than Sanchi
items.reasoning: Amaravati lies on the Krishna in Guntur district, in the lower reaches of the valley, so statement 1 is correct. The Amaravati school did have a long afterlife, in later South Indian sculpture and in images carried to Sri Lanka and South-east Asia, so statement 3 is correct. Statement 2 fails on measurement: the Amaravati Mahachaitya, at roughly fifty metres across, was larger than the Great Stupa at Sanchi, which is about thirty-seven metres, so Amaravati was not next after Sanchi in size. RUNNER-UP: D. D would win if the source the paper is drawn from states the Sanchi comparison in those words; a text that ranks Amaravati second to Sanchi in importance rather than in size would produce exactly this statement.

items.value: Only pair 2 is wrong: Udiyanjeral was a Chera, not a Chola
items.reasoning: Udiyanjeral, or Perunjeral Adan, is the Chera king of Sangam tradition celebrated for feeding both armies at Kurukshetra, so pairing him with the Cholas is incorrect. The other two are right: Senguttuvan is the Chera of the Silappadikaram who founded the Pattini cult, and Nedunjeliyan is the Pandya of Talaiyalanganam. The question asks which pairs are NOT correctly matched, so the answer is 2 only.

items.value: Gandhi's loss of confidence, the disunity of the Congress Left, and the preference of the Royists and Jayaprakash Narayan for Congress unity drove Bose to form the Forward Bloc
items.reasoning: Bose won the presidency at Tripuri in 1939 against Gandhi's candidate but could not carry Gandhi with him, and the Pant resolution then required him to nominate a Working Committee in accordance with Gandhi's wishes; his resignation and the founding of the Forward Bloc in May 1939 followed directly. The decisive weakness was that the Left was fragmented rather than behind him: M.N. Roy's followers opposed him outright and Jayaprakash Narayan's Congress Socialists stayed neutral, both in the name of preserving Congress unity. RUNNER-UP: A. Statement 3 is the pivot. The Communists deserted Bose at Tripuri, which makes it look true, but they had backed his candidature against Pattabhi Sitaramayya only weeks earlier, so a blanket claim that they did not support him is questionable; A wins if the examiner reads statement 3 as referring only to Tripuri and afterwards.

items.value: Statements 2 and 3 are correct; the taluqdars were disarmed and their forts destroyed, so statement 1 is wrong
items.reasoning: After the annexation of 1856 the taluqdars were not left in possession of their arms: their forts were demolished and their armed retainers disbanded, which is why statement 1 fails. The Summary Settlement of 1856 did proceed on the assumption that the taluqdars were interlopers with no permanent stake in the soil, who had established their hold by force and fraud, so statement 2 is correct. And the object of removing them was precisely to settle the revenue directly with the actual cultivating proprietors, which the British expected would both raise revenue and reduce the exploitation of peasants, so statement 3 is correct.

items.value: All three statements support the claim that community-based political alliances grew out of the design of the 1919 reforms
items.reasoning: The Montagu-Chelmsford scheme did not merely keep the separate electorates conceded in 1909 but widened them to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans, so statement 1 shows the communal principle written into the reforms themselves. Statement 2 supplies the intent behind that design, that separate representation was meant to blunt a nationalism the British found increasingly hard to contain, which is what makes the divisiveness inherent rather than accidental. Statement 3 supplies the mechanism by which the design produced alliances, since groups that stood to gain from communal representation organised themselves to claim it. RUNNER-UP: C. Statement 3 is the vulnerable one, because the Depressed Classes were given nominated seats in 1919 and did not receive separate electorates until the Communal Award of 1932; C wins if the examiner reads deprived classes strictly in that sense. A stricter reading still, that only statement 1 describes the nature of the reforms while 2 is motive and 3 is consequence, would give A.

items.value: Mallikarjun Mansur sang in the Jaipur-Atrauli gharana
items.reasoning: Mallikarjun Mansur of Karnataka, awarded the Bharat Ratna in 1992, is the best-known twentieth-century exponent of the Jaipur-Atrauli gharana, having trained under Manji Khan and then Burji Khan, the sons of Alladiya Khan who founded that gharana. His early training was in the Gwalior style, but his mature style and repertoire of rare ragas belong squarely to Jaipur-Atrauli.

items.value: The term kshetra-patni, mistress of the field, is traced to the Atharvaveda
items.reasoning: The Atharvaveda is the Vedic text most concerned with settled agriculture and with the household and its rituals, carrying the ploughing and sowing charms and the invocation of Sita, the personified furrow, so a feminine title for the presiding figure of a field belongs most naturally there. The Rigveda has the masculine kshetrapati, lord of the field, in its hymn to the field-deity, but not the feminine form. NOTE: this rests on a recalled attribution I am not certain of rather than on anything derivable from the stem, hence the low confidence. RUNNER-UP: C. The Ashtadhyayi is the text historians most often mine for socio-economic vocabulary of this kind, and Panini's rules on forming feminines in -patni would account for the word directly, so C wins if the paper is drawing on the Paninian evidence for women holding land. A is a weaker third: the Rigveda would win only if the examiner is treating the Kshetrapati hymn as also yielding the feminine.
